result.title: Diagnostic Performance of Agentic AI for Rare Disease Diagnosis: A Systematic Review, Meta-analysis, Workflow Development, and Benchmark-based Validation
result.authorString: Zheng C, Zhu J, Hu X, Wang C, Chen L.
result.abstractText: Background Rare diseases are characterized by diverse disease entities, heterogeneous phenotypes, complex diagnostic processes, and reliance on specialized expertise, resulting in substantial diagnostic delays. Large language models (LLMs) and Agentic artificial intelligence (Agentic AI) have recently been introduced into medical diagnosis. Compared with standalone LLMs, Agentic AI incorporates planning, external knowledge retrieval, iterative reasoning, and feedback mechanisms to improve complex diagnostic tasks. However, the overall diagnostic performance of Agentic AI in rare disease diagnosis and its transferable core workflows remain unclear. Methods A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted using PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, arXiv, and medRxiv/bioRxiv. Studies applying Agentic AI for rare disease diagnosis with extractable Top-1 diagnostic accuracy were included. Recall@1 was synthesized using a random effects single arm meta analysis, with leave-one-out sensitivity analysis. Agent capabilities were standardized using a unified capability taxonomy derived from existing agent frameworks. A lightweight workflow was subsequently constructed based on recurrently reported capabilities and evaluated using 50 randomly selected RareBench cases. The workflow-assisted Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) model was compared with the same model operating in standalone mode using Recall@1, Recall@3, and Recall@5. Results Seven studies contributing 19 effect estimates and 33,738 cases were included. The pooled Recall@1 was 51.2% (95% confidence interval [CI], 45.3% − 57.1%), and substantial heterogeneity was observed (I 2  = 98.5%). Leave-one-out analysis demonstrated robustness of the pooled estimate. Capability synthesis identified reasoning and hypothesis refinement and planning and task decomposition as the most consistently reported capabilities (7/7), followed by tool use and external knowledge integration and traceability and explainability (6/7). In RareBench validation, the workflow-assisted model improved Top-1 diagnosis compared with standalone GPT, achieving 11/50 correct diagnoses versus 5/50. Case level comparison showed that the workflow corrected 7 baseline errors, whereas baseline performance was superior in 1 case (exact McNemar test, P = 0.0703). Conclusions Agentic AI has demonstrated a certain level of diagnostic performance in rare disease diagnosis. However, diagnostic performance varies across different agent systems. In this study, we integrated the workflows reported in the included studies. The resulting workflow incorporates structured reasoning, external knowledge retrieval, and evidence tracking. This approach may provide a reproducible method for improving large language model based diagnostic systems. Future studies should develop more comprehensive workflows and conduct larger scale external validation. Ablation studies are also needed to determine the specific contribution of each agentic capability.

result.title: Conceptualising Health Economic Models Using a Graph Retrieval-Augmented, Agentic AI Framework with Human-in-the-Loop Validation: Proof-of-Concept Study.

result.abstractText:
Objective

Health economic models (HEMs) are crucial for assessing the cost-effectiveness of healthcare interventions, informing policy decisions and guiding reimbursement strategies. This study examines the feasibility of employing generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) for the conceptualisation of HEMs. Two proof-of-concept studies were conducted, implementing a first-of-its-kind agentic Gen-AI-augmented approach for model conceptualisation.

Methods

An agentic Gen-AI framework was developed, incorporating the chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning algorithm through advanced prompt engineering, compounded with self-consistency, executed in an external Python programming environment. Within this framework, an agentic execution layer (the 'agent') autonomously orchestrated a multi-step retrieval-reasoning-generation task. Additionally, a graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) technique was implemented by linking the large language model (LLM) to an external database curated with user-selected data specific to HEM. Two case studies were explored: breast cancer, representing a data-rich disease area, and transthyretin amyloid polyneuropathy (ATTR-PN), exemplifying a data-sparse rare disease.

Results

The agentic Gen-AI framework successfully generated two key outputs that were subsequently validated against published literature and expert review from health economic (HE) modelers and clinicians: (1) a disease concept diagram illustrating the progression of the disease and its associated health states, and (2) a model structure diagram depicting patient transitions between various health states.

Conclusions

The findings suggest that Gen-AI-augmented methodologies can enhance multiple aspects of HEM conceptualisation, including problem definition, disease and treatment effect pathway development, model structure recommendations, and drafting of model specification plans. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first study to integrate cutting-edge Gen-AI techniques such as human-in-the-loop (HITL), chain of thought-self-consistency (CoT-SC), and graph-based RAG for HEM conceptualisation or broader health economics and outcomes research (HEOR) applications.

result.title: Artificial intelligence agents and agentic artificial intelligence applied to precision medicine.

result.abstractText: Precision medicine seeks to individualise care by integrating multimodal biomedical data, yet most deployed clinical artificial intelligence (AI) remains assistive, providing predictions without managing workflows or adapting autonomously. Agentic AI, built on large language models (LLMs), has emerged as a paradigm characterised by autonomy, goal-directed reasoning, memory, planning and tool use. This review synthesises evidence on agentic AI and LLMs applied to precision medicine, encompassing drug discovery, genomics, oncology, rare disease diagnostics and clinical pharmacology. This review also examines architectural components, recent validation milestones and emerging challenges, including hallucination, sociodemographic bias and evolving regulatory frameworks across the FDA, the EU AI Act and the WHO.

result.abstractText: Biomedical research is increasingly constrained by repetitive, fragmented workflows that slow discovery. We introduce Biomni, a general-purpose biomedical artificial intelligence agent that autonomously executes diverse research tasks. To map the biomedical action space, Biomni's action-discovery agent mines tools, databases, and protocols from thousands of publications across 25 domains, building a unified agentic environment. Its general-purpose architecture integrates large language model reasoning with retrieval-augmented planning and code-based execution, dynamically composing workflows without predefined templates. Systematic benchmarking shows strong generalization across heterogeneous tasks-causal gene prioritization, drug repurposing, rare-disease diagnosis, microbiome analysis, and molecular cloning-without task-specific tuning. Real-world case studies demonstrate Biomni interpreting multimodal datasets, optimizing protein stability, orchestrating wet-lab instruments, and generating experimentally testable protocols. Biomni envisions artificial intelligence augmenting human scientists and accelerating discovery.
